Mapping large datasets

Source: vignettes/plotting.Rmd
plotting.Rmd

Drawing a hexagon for every cell becomes slow long before you run out of data: a million cells means a million polygons. globalhex avoids this by keeping data as cell IDs and building polygons only for the cells that end up on the screen.

library(globalhex)

Cell data

hex_data() pairs a vector of cells with one or more columns of values. It is a tibble, and it contains no geometry:

storms <- dplyr::storms
cells <- point_to_cell(storms[c("long", "lat")], resolution = 6)

x <- hex_data(cells, wind = storms$wind, observations = 1L)
x
#> # A tibble: 20,778 × 3
#>    cell       wind observations
#>    <gh_cell> <int>        <int>
#>  1 02004556     25            1
#>  2 02004530     25            1
#>  3 02004134     25            1
#>  4 02000401     25            1
#>  5 02000004     25            1
#>  6 02000031     25            1
#>  7 02000335     25            1
#>  8 02003634     30            1
#>  9 02003265     35            1
#> 10 02034445     40            1
#> # ℹ 20,768 more rows

A cell can appear many times. Here each row is one storm observation, and several observations fall in the same cell.

Plotting

plot() draws a hex_data object. Use value to choose a column (the first one is used by default):

plot(x, value = "wind", resolution = 4)

Before drawing, values are summarized from the data’s resolution up to the display resolution. The summary depends on the column type:

Column type Default summary
numeric mean
logical majority
character or factor most common value

Counts and other totals should be added up instead, with fun = sum:

plot(x, value = "observations", fun = sum, resolution = 4, border = NA)

Choosing the display resolution

If you leave out resolution, globalhex picks the finest resolution whose visible cells fit on the current device at a few pixels each. plot_resolution() reports what it would choose:

plot_resolution(x)
#> [1] 6

You can steer the automatic choice instead of fixing it:

  • max_cells caps the number of cells drawn.
  • cell_pixels sets the smallest cell size, in screen pixels.
  • lod = FALSE turns off automatic aggregation and draws the data at its own resolution.
plot(x, value = "wind", max_cells = 2000)

Zooming in

extent (or the familiar xlim and ylim) limits the map to a longitude/latitude window. Cells outside it are dropped before aggregation, so zooming in allows finer detail. Use reset = FALSE to keep drawing on the same map afterwards, here to add coastlines:

world <- sf::st_as_sf(maps::map("world", plot = FALSE, fill = TRUE))

plot(x, value = "observations", fun = sum, resolution = 5,
     xlim = c(-98, -76), ylim = c(17, 32), reset = FALSE)
plot(sf::st_geometry(world), add = TRUE, border = "black", lwd = 0.6)

For a window that crosses the 180° meridian, give an extent whose xmin is larger than its xmax, such as c(170, -170, -10, 10).

Map projections

Set crs to any projection understood by sf::st_crs(). Values are summarized first and only the final cells are projected:

temperature <- terra::rast(nrows = 180, ncols = 360)
xy <- terra::xyFromCell(temperature, seq_len(terra::ncell(temperature)))
terra::values(temperature) <- 30 * cos(xy[, 2] * pi / 180) - 10
names(temperature) <- "temperature"

global <- raster_to_cell(temperature, resolution = 4, progress = FALSE)
global
#> # A tibble: 24,012 × 2
#>    cell      temperature
#>    <gh_cell>       <dbl>
#>  1 000000           5.78
#>  2 010000           5.78
#>  3 010003           5.21
#>  4 010036           4.65
#>  5 010032           4.08
#>  6 010345           3.50
#>  7 010341           2.90
#>  8 010304           2.30
#>  9 010300           1.69
#> 10 010303           1.09
#> # ℹ 24,002 more rows

plot(global, crs = "+proj=eqearth")

Large maps

Drawing thousands of separate polygons is slow on most graphics devices and produces very large PDF or SVG files. When more than 20,000 cells would be drawn and terra is installed, plot() therefore draws them as a single image instead. The render argument controls this:

  • "auto" (default) chooses based on raster_threshold.
  • "polygon" always draws separate polygons, which you need for cell borders.
  • "raster" always draws an image.

Summarizing without plotting

cell_aggregate() performs the same summary as plot() and returns the result, so you can analyze it or plot it another way:

coarse <- cell_aggregate(x, resolution = 3, fun = sum, value = "observations")
coarse[order(-coarse$observations), ]
#> # A tibble: 353 × 2
#>    cell      observations
#>    <gh_cell>        <dbl>
#>  1 02000              262
#>  2 02534              258
#>  3 02526              221
#>  4 02521              218
#>  5 02522              207
#>  6 02006              206
#>  7 02034              205
#>  8 02423              203
#>  9 02004              202
#> 10 02063              202
#> # ℹ 343 more rows

To use other plotting tools, such as ggplot2, convert the cells to polygons with sf::st_as_sf(). Aggregate first so that you only build the polygons you need:

polygons <- sf::st_as_sf(coarse$cell)
polygons$observations <- coarse$observations

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(polygons) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = observations), color = NA)

sf::st_as_sf() prepares the polygons for flat longitude/latitude maps. Cells that cross the 180° meridian are split into two parts, one at each edge of the map, and cells containing a pole are closed along the top or bottom edge. Areas from sf::st_area() are unchanged. For a Pacific-centred map, shift the longitudes to 0–360° with sf::st_shift_longitude():

pacific <- sf::st_shift_longitude(polygons)

Use sf::st_as_sf(cells, wrap = FALSE) to get the unsplit spherical polygons, for example to project them to a polar map yourself.
